"Implement the solution in src/main/java/VariableLengthQuantity.java so that the tests in src/test/java/VariableLengthQuantityTest.java pass. The specification follows.

# Instructions

Implement variable length quantity encoding and decoding.

The goal of this exercise is to implement [VLQ][vlq] encoding/decoding.

In short, the goal of this encoding is to encode integer values in a way that would save bytes.
Only the first 7 bits of each byte are significant (right-justified; sort of like an ASCII byte).
So, if you have a 32-bit value, you have to unpack it into a series of 7-bit bytes.
Of course, you will have a variable number of bytes depending upon your integer.
To indicate which is the last byte of the series, you leave bit #7 clear.
In all of the preceding bytes, you set bit #7.

So, if an integer is between `0-127`, it can be represented as one byte.
Although VLQ can deal with numbers of arbitrary sizes, for this exercise we will restrict ourselves to only numbers that fit in a 32-bit unsigned integer.
Here are examples of integers as 32-bit values, and the variable length quantities that they translate to:

```text
 NUMBER        VARIABLE QUANTITY
00000000              00
00000040              40
0000007F              7F
00000080             81 00
00002000             C0 00
00003FFF             FF 7F
00004000           81 80 00
00100000           C0 80 00
001FFFFF           FF FF 7F
00200000          81 80 80 00
08000000          C0 80 80 00
0FFFFFFF          FF FF FF 7F
```

[vlq]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variable-length_quantity


Do NOT modify the tests or the build files except as stated below. Do not create new files unless the specification requires them; Helper classes may go only in the solution's package."

content.text: First, let's take a look at the test file and the existing solution file.

The tests use `new VariableLengthQuantity()` from the default package — the class is package-private, but since the tests are also in the default package, it's fine.

Implementation:

encode: For each number, extract 7-bit groups from the least significant bits, set the continuation bit (0x80) on all but the last group, and format in lowercase hex as "0x%02x".

decode: Accumulate 7 bits, and if the continuation bit is set, shift left by 7. If the input runs out before the continuation bit is cleared, throw an IllegalArgumentException with the message "Invalid variable-length quantity encoding".

Hex format: Output like "0x0", "0x40", "0x7f" — lowercase, no leading zeros other than the "0x" prefix. Use String.format("0x%x", value).

Wait — there's a subtle issue with the decode: if the last byte has the continuation bit set, it throws an exception. But what if the sequence ends with a continuation bit set mid-list? That can't happen — if a byte has the continuation bit set, the sequence continues; the only way for the input to end is if the last byte has it set. That's handled. But there's another edge case: what if the last byte has the continuation bit set AND it's the final byte? Handled. What about the case where the input ends exactly on a completed sequence? No problem.

Alright, let's run the tests.

All tests pass. I implemented `src/main/java/VariableLengthQuantity.java`:

- **`encode`**: For each number, it splits the value into 7-bit groups starting from the least significant bits, sets the continuation bit (`0x80`) on every group except the last, and emits each group as a lowercase hex string (`0x%x`).
- **`decode`**: It accumulates each byte's low 7 bits, shifting left by 7 per group. When a byte lacks the continuation bit, the accumulated value is emitted. If the input ends while a sequence is still open (continuation bit set on the last byte), it throws `IllegalArgumentException("Invalid variable-length quantity encoding")`.

`./gradlew test` reports a successful build with all 23 tests passing.
